analysis.one_liner: Lets laid-off workers recover up to $20,000 in unpaid wages and benefits ahead of other creditors in bankruptcy.
analysis.headline: The bill died in a House Judiciary subcommittee without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: When a company goes bankrupt, employees owed back pay, sick leave, or severance are supposed to be paid ahead of many other creditors, but current law caps those claims at $4,000 and only counts wages earned in the final 90 days. This bill would raise the cap to $20,000, drop the 90-day limit, and give employees owed WARN Act notice pay — the money owed when a plant closes without 60 days' warning — a high-priority place in line ahead of most unsecured creditors. It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to a subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers whose employers go bankrupt owing them wages, vacation, sick leave, severance, or health benefits — especially at companies that close without the 60-day layoff notice the WARN Act requires. They would recover up to five times more from the bankrupt estate, and their claims would rank ahead of ordinary unsecured creditors.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Employees owed pay by bankrupt employers

how_it_helps.text: Raises the priority cap for employee wage and benefit claims in bankruptcy from $4,000 to $20,000, so workers recover more of what they are owed before other creditors are paid.
Removes the 90-day lookback, so wages earned earlier before the bankruptcy filing also count toward the priority claim.
Gives employees' WARN Act claims — compensation owed when a plant closes or mass layoff happens without required advance notice — fifth priority in bankruptcy, ahead of most unsecured creditors.

analysis.who_pays: Banks, bondholders, trade creditors, and other lenders who lend to or do business with struggling companies. In a bankruptcy, every dollar that goes to employees ahead of them is a dollar they do not recover, which can translate into tighter terms on lending to weak firms.

drawbacks.text: Shifting more of a limited bankruptcy estate to employees means unsecured creditors — including suppliers and small businesses owed money by the failed company — recover less, and lenders may charge more or lend less to financially shaky employers as compensation for that risk.

The bill made its changes apply to bankruptcy cases begun after January 1, 2004, so employees of companies that had already filed would get nothing, and its immediate effect would be retroactive in effect on estates in progress.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would put substantially more of a bankrupt employer's remaining money into the hands of workers who were never paid, at a cost spread thinly across lenders and other creditors who price that risk into their lending. It did nothing for employees of companies that had already filed, and it was never revised or debated after introduction.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to its Commercial and Administrative Law subcommittee, which never acted on it, and it died when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Rep. Luis Gutierrez introduced the bill on February 11, 2004, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.
On March 1, 2004, it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Commercial and Administrative Law, and no further action was taken for the rest of the Congress.
The bill had no cosponsors and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Lenders and other unsecured creditors are better off, because employee claims in bankruptcy remain capped at $4,000 with the 90-day limit intact, leaving more of a bankrupt company's assets for them. The bill also competed for attention in the same period as the broader 2005 bankruptcy overhaul, which was moving separately.

for.name: Rep. Luis Gutierrez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor; it drew no cosponsors.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after receiving the referral.

against.name: House Judiciary Subcommittee on Commercial and Administrative Law
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on March 1, 2004, and took no action for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never advanced far enough to reveal a partisan split: it had a single Democratic sponsor, no cosponsors of either party, and no votes were ever taken on it.

industries.note: The bill would move up to $20,000 per employee of unpaid wages and benefits, plus WARN Act claims, ahead of lenders in the bankruptcy line, reducing what they recover from failed corporate borrowers. Its failure preserves the current cap and the lenders' place in line.

Every priority dollar paid to employees comes out of the pool available to unsecured creditors, including suppliers and bondholders of the failed company. The bill's death leaves their recoveries unchanged.
